Wealthy
welth'y
a. (rich; having large possessions; and in the Authorized Version, of a place of abundance and security)
From wealth, Saxon wela, weal, welfare, prosperity — the older English sense being well-being generally, of which money is only one part.

Biblical Definition

Both occurrences of wealthy in the Authorized Version describe a place, not a person, and they land on opposite sides of the ledger. The first is deliverance: “Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place” (Psa 66:12). The wealthy place is what lies on the far side of the fire and the water; it is the end of a providence, not an escape from one. The second is indictment: “Arise, get you up unto the wealthy nation, that dwelleth without care, saith the LORD, which have neither gates nor bars, which dwell alone” (Jer 49:31). Kedar is wealthy and careless, unwalled because it fears nothing, and the LORD is sending Nebuchadrezzar to it. Put the two together and the doctrine is plain: wealth as God's gift at the end of a trial is a mercy to be sung about; wealth as a settled condition that removes the sense of need is a summons. Proverbs keeps the same edge on both sides — “He that trusteth in his riches shall fall: but the righteous shall flourish as a branch” (Pro 11:28) — and warns that the accounts are not what they look like: “There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches” (Pro 13:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines wealthy as rich; having large possessions in lands, goods, money or securities; opulent; affluent.

expand to see more

WEALTH'Y, a. welth'y. [from wealth.]

1. Rich; having large possessions in lands, goods, money or securities, or larger than the generality of men; opulent; affluent.

It is often synonymous with rich, but rich may denote a greater degree of opulence.

2. Abundant; ample; as a wealthy place.

Thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place. Ps. 66.

Key Scripture

Psalm 66:12 — "Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place."

Jeremiah 49:31 — "Arise, get you up unto the wealthy nation, that dwelleth without care, saith the LORD, which have neither gates nor bars, which dwell alone."

Proverbs 11:28 — "He that trusteth in his riches shall fall: but the righteous shall flourish as a branch."

Proverbs 13:7 — "There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches."

Modern Corruption

Prosperity preaching claims Psalm 66:12 and skips the fire and the water; the ascetic claims Jeremiah 49:31 and forgets it was carelessness, not wealth, that was judged.

expand to see more

Psalm 66:12 is a favourite verse of prosperity teaching, always quoted from the comma forward. The whole verse has men riding over the psalmist's head, and fire, and water, and only then the wealthy place — and God is the subject of every clause including the riding. A promise of the destination that suppresses the road is not the psalm; it is an advertisement using the psalm's words. Job, Joseph, and Paul all reached wealthy places by exactly this route, and none of them could have sold tickets for it.

The opposite error treats Jeremiah 49:31 as a verdict on money itself. Read it again: the charge against Kedar is dwelling without care, with neither gates nor bars, alone — a security so complete it has stopped looking up. That is a condition of soul available at any income. The Reformed doctrine of vocation holds that wealth is a stewardship with an account to render, that trusting it is the fall (Pro 11:28), and that the books as men keep them are frequently the reverse of the books as God keeps them (Pro 13:7).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew revayah (H7310), abundance, saturation; Hebrew shalev (H7961), at ease, careless; Saxon wela, weal, welfare.

expand to see more

Hebrew revayah (H7310) — overflowing abundance, saturation; the wealthy place of Psalm 66:12, a watered land after fire.

Hebrew shalev (H7961) — quiet, at ease, careless; the wealthy nation of Jeremiah 49:31, and the word carries the rebuke.

Saxon wela — weal, well-being; the older English in which wealth meant welfare and not only money.

Hebrew hon (H1952) — substance, riches; the noun in Proverbs 11:28 and 13:7.

Greek euporia (G2142) — wealth, plenty; Acts 19:25, where a craft's wealth resists the gospel.

Usage

"“Through fire and through water… into a wealthy place” — the road is part of the promise."

"“The wealthy nation, that dwelleth without care” — unwalled, unafraid, and summoned."

"“Maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches” — the ledgers do not agree."
